article.title: ChainDrop Worm Hijacks keyv and cacheable npm Packages, Spreading to 440 Packages in Under Four Hours
article.summary: A compromised maintainer account let a self-propagating worm called ChainDrop poison the keyv and cacheable npm package families, hitting 440 packages with over 500 million weekly downloads.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

A self-propagating malware campaign dubbed ChainDrop spread through the npm JavaScript package registry on August 4, 2026, after attackers compromised the GitHub account of the maintainer behind the widely used `keyv` and `cacheable` package families. According to [Microsoft Security Blog](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/), Microsoft Threat Intelligence "identified a large-scale npm supply chain attack affecting more than 400 packages across multiple unrelated publishers, including packages associated with major enterprise software ecosystems such as keyv, flat-cache, cache-manager, and others."

## What We Know

According to [Aikido Security](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/keyv-and-friends-compromised-in-npm-supply-chain-attack), attackers compromised the GitHub account of the maintainer behind `keyv` — "a key-value storage library with roughly 127 million weekly npm downloads" — and used that access to inject a credential-stealing worm across the package family. [Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/blog/keyv-and-cacheable-npm-supply-chain-attack) reports the attack was "initiated at 9:00 UTC via compromised GitHub maintainer account."

Aikido describes the mechanics of the initial compromise: "The compromise was carried out by pushing malicious files directly to the main branch and then immediately cutting a new release, meaning the poisoned versions were published to npm with valid provenance signed by GitHub Actions." The first poisoned release was `keyv@6.0.0`.

According to [Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/08/04/chaindrop-supply-chain-compromise-anatomy-self-propagating-worm/), "the malicious releases contain a Mini Shai-Hulud variant, a self-propagating credential-stealing worm delivered through a large, heavily obfuscated Bun-based JavaScript payload." [StepSecurity](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/chaindrop-npm-worm) reports the dropper "downloads the legitimate Bun JavaScript runtime, straight from the official oven-sh/bun GitHub releases," rather than shipping its own binary, and uses it to run the obfuscated second-stage payload. StepSecurity names the compromised maintainer as "jaredwray," with poisoned commits pushed to the `jaredwray/keyv`, `jaredwray/cacheable`, and `jaredwray/ecto` repositories.

Once it runs, the malware goes looking for credentials broadly. Microsoft states that "once executed, the malware searches developer workstations and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) environments for npm, GitHub, cloud, and infrastructure credentials." Wiz's analysis lists targeted platforms including "AI platforms (Claude, OpenAI, Codex, Cursor, Gemini)" alongside cloud providers, developer tools, and CI/CD systems, and StepSecurity separately confirms the payload hunts for "AI tool credentials" such as `.claude/credentials.json`, `.cursor/credentials.json`, and `.openai/auth.json`. For persistence, Microsoft says the malware achieves this partly through "injection into Claude configuration files" and "injection into Visual Studio Code configuration files," a mechanism Wiz separately describes as writing to "Claude Code hooks" and "VS Code tasks.json."

The worm's command-and-control setup avoids a fixed domain. [SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/over-400-npm-packages-infected-in-chaindrop-supply-chain-attack/) reports the malware "uses an Ethereum blockchain for command-and-control (C&C), a technique called EtherHiding," a detail StepSecurity corroborates, noting the worm's C2 address "is resolved from the Ethereum blockchain." Microsoft separately lists observed exfiltration infrastructure including the domain `npm-cache[.]com`.

SecurityWeek describes how the malware spread on its own, quoting security firm JFrog: "After obtaining an NPM publishing token, it enumerates packages available to the compromised identity, downloads their latest tarballs, inserts the malware and setup loader, adds a preinstall hook, increments the patch version, and republishes the modified packages." That mechanism is what let the campaign expand well beyond the maintainer's own packages.

On scale, SecurityWeek reports the campaign "started with 11 malware carriers in the keyv and cacheable namespaces," before growing rapidly: "more than 2,200 malicious versions of 440 packages were published to the NPM registry," with "the total number of malicious package iterations observed on August 4" reaching "2,212 in under four hours." SecurityWeek adds that this self-propagation caused "433 additional packages" to be infected as secondary victims, and that "combined, the infected packages have over 500 million weekly downloads."

On the question of npm's provenance system, which is meant to let developers verify where a package build came from, [Snyk](https://snyk.io/blog/inside-keyv-npm-compromise-preinstall-malware-trusted-provenance-ide-hooks/) offered this assessment: "Provenance remains valuable evidence about build origin. This incident shows its boundary: provenance can faithfully attest a build whose source or workflow context has already been compromised." Snyk also confirmed the malicious install hook runs through the standard npm lifecycle mechanism, with a `package.json` entry reading `"preinstall": "node setup.mjs"`.

For remediation, JFrog's guidance as carried by SecurityWeek is to "isolate affected systems" and "preserve package tarballs, npm logs, CI logs, GitHub audit logs, and runner images before cleanup" — advice aimed at organizations that may need to investigate before restoring systems to service.

## What We Don't Know

None of the sources reviewed disclose how the attacker initially obtained the maintainer's GitHub credentials. It is also not yet clear how many organizations were compromised as a direct result of installing the poisoned packages, as opposed to how many packages carried the malicious code — package download counts measure exposure, not confirmed compromise.

## Context

ChainDrop is the latest in a series of self-propagating npm worms tracing back to the Shai-Hulud malware family. The Machine Herald [previously reported](/article/2026-05/18-mini-shai-hulud-worm-hits-tanstack-mistral-ai-and-uipath-compromising-170-npm-and-pypi-packages-with-518m-combined-downloads) on a related "Mini" Shai-Hulud campaign that hit npm and PyPI packages tied to TanStack, Mistral AI, and UiPath in May 2026. Microsoft's classification of the ChainDrop payload as a "Mini Shai-Hulud variant," and Wiz's description of it as a "descendant of the 'Mini' Shai-Hulud malware family," place this incident in that same lineage of worms that specifically target npm's lifecycle-hook install mechanism to spread automatically once they gain a foothold.
